summary: Describes the file format used to store facsimile (fax) images from the Rapicom 450 fax machine. It is a memo aimed at people who needed to handle that machine's data on their own computers.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC documents how Rapicom 450 fax machines package their encoded image blocks into files. It lets organizations with compatible equipment interpret the record sequence.

questions: how was fax data stored in early networks
what is the rapicom 450 file format
subtitle: The record layout used to store Rapicom 450 facsimile data in files.

tldr.problem: Organizations with Rapicom 450 machines needed a documented way to exchange stored facsimile data.
tldr.mechanism: The file stores setup, data, and end records, each with a length byte, command byte, and data bytes.
tldr.outcome: The 585-bit blocks retain the Rapicom 450 encoding and are not directly usable as a bitmap without its decoding procedure.

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 769 an Unknown status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the File Format Is Documented
sections.content:
Organizations had connected Rapicom 450 facsimile machines to computers so they could save a page as a file and produce it later. They could exchange the stored data through file transfer and other protocols.

This memo records the file format so other organizations with compatible facsimile devices can join that exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo explains how to recognize files made by a particular fax machine. It is for systems with compatible equipment.

sections.title: Record Layout and Commands
sections.content:
The Rapicom 450 produces encoded blocks of 585 bits. Each block is stored in a record of eight-bit bytes: a length byte, a command byte, and data bytes. The length includes the first two bytes, and the command identifies the data.

Command 56 marks setup data, 57 marks a data block, and 58 marks the final record. An end record may have length 2 and no data.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record starts with its size and a code that says whether it contains setup information, image data, or the end marker.

sections.title: File Sequence and Encoded Blocks
sections.content:
A file begins with one SET-UP record, continues with DATA records, and ends with an END record. In files exchanged at the time, each record carries one block; the data field is 74 bytes and the usual record length is 76.

The first 24 bits of a block are a synchronization mark. The next byte carries a sequence number in its low two bits, cycling through 11, 01, 10, and 00 starting with the first DATA record. The encoded data requires the Rapicom 450 encoding and decoding procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup record comes first, image records follow, and an end record closes the file. The image bits follow the machine's encoding, so they need its decoding method.
